Describes a range of businesses based on the number of employees or annual turnover.
SMEs represent the vast majority of businesses in Australia, employ millions of people, and are the engine of the economy, responsible for 55% of GDP.

The business structure chosen, needs to meet the needs of the owner(s) and depends on these key factors:
Size: how large will the business be / grow to?
Tax: how can the owner(s) minimise their tax burden (the amount of tax they need to pay)?
Ownership: how much control would the owner(s) like over the business?
Liability / Risk: how much protection would the business like from risk? E.g. financial/legal risk
Succession: who will take over when the owner(s) are gone?
Finance: where will the business get its starting capital?
pg 1-2

A type of enterprise owned and run by one person and in which there is no legal distinction between the owner and the business entity.
A sole trader does not necessarily work alone and may employ other people.
pg 3

A partnership is a business structure made up of 2 or more people who distribute income or losses between themselves.
There is no legal distinction between the owners and the business entity.
pg 3

A company, and the entities it controls, with fewer than 50 employees.
There is a legal distinction between the owners and the business entity.
pg 3

A not-for-profit is an organisation that does not operate for the profit, personal gain or other benefit of the owner(s) or shareholders, but rather, the profit must be reinvested in the business and its mission.
There is a legal distinction between the owners and the business entity.
pg 3

A an arrangement where the franchisor (creator), licences the business model to franchisees (the owners), in return for ongoing fees/royalties.
Franchises (the original business) can be held in the structure of a sole trader, partnership or small proprietary company.

Compare control, liability, finance, continuity and purpose. A not-for-profit can earn a surplus, but applies it to its purpose rather than distributing it as profit to members.

Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level. A business may face rising wages, rent, materials and delivery costs. If it cannot raise selling prices proportionately, its profit margin can fall.

Consumers’ real purchasing power falls when their incomes do not keep pace with prices. A café may see customers choose smaller purchases or cheaper substitutes. Analyse both the cost effect on the café and the demand effect from its customers.

Higher interest rates increase repayments on variable-rate borrowing and can make new investment less attractive. They can also reduce consumers’ disposable income after loan repayments, weakening demand.
A furniture retailer considering a second store should compare expected sales, financing costs and the risk of lower demand. A lower interest rate does not guarantee an investment will succeed.

A shortage of skilled workers can delay production, raise recruitment costs and increase wage pressure. Training, apprenticeships, retention and changes to work organisation can help, but take time and resources.

Higher unemployment can reduce aggregate consumer spending and make recruitment easier in some occupations. An unemployed person’s skills and location may still differ from those a business needs. Distinguish the unemployment rate from the availability of a particular skill.

PEST groups external influences into political/legal, economic, socio-cultural and technological factors. Explain how a factor changes a specific business decision rather than merely naming the factor.

Example: rising interest rates increase a bakery’s equipment-finance cost. The owner compares leasing, delaying expansion and purchasing a smaller machine. A justified recommendation considers capacity, cash flow, customer demand and risk.

‘The market’ is a figurative place, where buyers and sellers exchange of goods and services for money.
It is a system of exchange between consumers and producers (businesses).
The activity of promoting and selling products or services to the market.

Increases Brand Awareness: Marketing assists businesses to raise awareness for their brand (and their products!) in the minds of consumers so that they are more likely to purchase them
Increases Market Share: Marketing helps businesses to win more of the market away from competing brands e.g. McDonald's holds a 30% market share of the cheeseburger market in Australia.
Increases Sales & Revenue: Increasing marketing efforts often results in an increase in sales, which produces increased revenue for the business.

The function of a business is to operate and make a profit. Business functions is correlated with the health of a business.
The health of business can be measured in a variety of ways, including:
Revenue
Expenses
Profit
Quality of Goods and Services
Desirability as an Employer
etc…

Revenue = Total Sales
Expenses = Total Costs
Profit = Revenue - Expenses

Market size is the number of potential buyers there are for a product
e.g. Baby Nappies market size is 250,000 families in Australia, each week.
This is estimated by a business to determine:
their market share,
whether new product ideas are ‘viable’ (going to make money and be worth pursuing).

Market share is the proportion of all buyers, that purchase from one particular brand
e.g. Baby Nappies market size is 250,000 families in Australia, each week. Huggies hace 17% market share (42,500 families/week).

This is estimated by a business to determine:
Their greatest competitors
Their strength in against other brands (can they set price? Can they introduce new products? Will consumers stay loyal to them?)
Their estimated annual revenue
etc…

Therefore: while market size simply measures the number of potential customers, market share measures the number of customers, out of the potential pool of customers, who purchase from one particular company.

Markets are very large and potential buyers have very diverse needs and wants, so not all of them would ‘suit’ the products that a business has to offer.
Therefore, businesses must decide: Who is our target market?
Markets segmentation is where a business divides a market of potential customers into different segments, and chooses a particular ‘segment’ to target with their product.

Markets can be segmented by:
Demographic characteristics
Geographic characteristics
Psychographic characteristics

Examples of demographic segmentation include:
Age
Race
Gender
Ethnicity
Religion
Income
Education
Marital status
Family size
“who”

Examples of geographic segmentation include:
Location
Culture
Language
Tradition
“where”

Examples of psychographic segmentation include:
Values
Desires
Goals
Interests
Lifestyle choices
“how”

If everyone is your customer: no one is your customer
This is based on the idea that customers have:
Specific wants and needs that they are seeking to satisfy with products
Choice of different products from different businesses
This is why businesses make each product slightly different, aimed at satisfying different needs/wants.
The greater the level of competition in the market (the higher the number of businesses offering competing products), the more tailored the product needs to be, to be successful.

Well-segmented and targeted market:
Higher sales and increased revenue
Greater advertising effectiveness, reducing the cost of promotion per purchase
Increased profit, based on increased revenue and decreased cost

Poorly-segmented and targeted market:
Weak sales and decreased revenue
Ineffective advertising, increasing the cost of promotion per purchase
Reduced profit, based on decreased revenue and increased cost

Customer profiling is a marketing strategy that uses data to create a picture of the ideal customer who will interact with your product or service.

A well-researched, useful customer profile will guide the marketing and advertising of a product, to reach your ideal customers and achieve the business’ objectives.

bme-y11-u1-competitor-profiling.title: Marketing Strategy: High Volume, Low Price

blocks.text:
A high volume, low price strategy is where a business is focussed on making sales and increasing market share.
Their profit margin is typically low per product, although they are increasing their brand salience and leveraging WoM.

bme-y11-u1-competitor-profiling.title: Marketing Strategy: Low Volume, High Price

blocks.text:
A low volume, high price strategy is where a business is focussed on increasing profit margin and establishing or maintaining a premium brand image.
Their profit margin is typically very high per product, and their marketing mix positions the product as special / superior in quality.
Lamborghini sold 131 vehicles during 2021.In 2022, Ford sold 66,628 vehicles in Australia.
